coherence.reasons: Both run the same broad chain: the opportunity, why retail-led fails, the Amazon-led case and its condition, then the plan. X's governing thought carries the binding condition (payback only below 28.6% ACoS), and every section builds toward the gates and the go/no-go, so the top line matches what the body proves. Y's governing thought says Amazon-first is 'the only route inside the board's limits', yet its own options table shows Japan passing every limit; the condition appears only lower down. Y's sectioning is cleaner (economics separated from input realism, backup tables), while X files the Japan comparison and the 2029 retail-layer test somewhat awkwardly under other headings. On balance X's hierarchy is slightly more consistent from top to bottom.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred recommendation (Amazon-led with gates, retail deferred to above 20% awareness, ambition about $26M) and both reject Option B on the cap, payback and margin floor. X weighs the alternatives more fully. It quantifies the US-versus-Japan trade-off (Japan returns more cash above 25.9% ACoS, which is below the pilot's 28%) and still argues for the US on the size of business built. It turns Japan into an explicit fallback tied to a go/no-go at end-2027, commits only to the 2027 launch, and sizes the cash envelope to the worst case ($3.9M) rather than the cap. It also tests a staged national retail layer in 2029 and shows it breaks payback (−$11.9M) and the margin floor (6.3%), then proposes costing a regional test. Y states the ambition reset more explicitly in the recommendation and adds a tariff-response guardrail. But Y dismisses Japan on revenue alone ('adds little'), gives no consequence if the ACoS guardrail is breached, and leaves phase-2 retail as 'needs its own case' without numbers.

evidence.reasons: The core numbers are identical and match the key in both: Option B −$20.8M and 4.5% margin, Option A at 25/28/32% ACoS giving $2.40M/$0.38M/−$2.32M, break-even 28.6% (26.9% with the tariff), −$26.4M for B at 2.6 units and no halo, $26.4M and $37.6M of 2030 revenue. Both exclude the $5.2B figure, reject the halo correlation as non-causal, and note that two of three Amazon-first entrants stalled. Y shows more of the required working explicitly: retail contribution of $7.54 per unit, Amazon contribution before ads of $10.7, Option A margin by year and full backup tables. X adds correct extra analyses that bear on the decision: the 25.9% Japan crossover, the −$11.9M retail-layer case, the $3.9M worst-case peak, the 32 units per door needed to cover retail fixed cost, and the point that a quarter of brands above 20% awareness still sell 3.9 or less. Y has a few soft overreaches: 'Onsoo's 48% in Korea shows the headroom' leans toward the Korean-repeat trap; Mooncrest was 'removed after the retailer's review' is not in the pack; and 'stores would delist it' is stated as certain. X is more cautious ('loyalty is not yet proven', 'likely removed'), with only a trivial unsupported aside that fees are 'fixed by contract'. Net, a narrow edge to X.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's Amazon-first hypothesis and add conditions, as the key expects. Both tighten the retail trigger from 15% to 20% awareness, using the 3.5 units against the 4.0 delisting line, and both add the ACoS payback condition. Y labels the change explicitly as a revision of the CEO's gate and restates the ambition. X goes further on the second half of the hypothesis: it models 'add national retail from 2029' on top of Option A and shows that, even at 4.5 units per door, it leaves the US $11.9M short of payback and pushes group margin to 6.3%. So the retail step needs a different shape (a regional test) and a later payback date, not just a higher awareness gate. X also attaches a go/no-go with a Japan fallback if the ACoS condition fails. That is a more thorough, evidence-led update of the hypothesis.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, numerically sound answers that reach the defensible recommendation and avoid the main traps. Y is somewhat more transparent on unit economics and backup detail, and more explicit about restating the $40M ambition. X better equips the board to decide. It is candid that payback is marginal and that Japan beats the US on cash at the pilot's ACoS. It limits the commitment to 2027 with a defined go/no-go and a fallback. And it shows that the CEO's planned 2029 national retail step would itself break payback and the margin floor. Those are the points the board most needs when trading ambition against constraints.
